planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring, or direct sow fall-collected seed for natural cold stratification, into dry to average, well-drained soil in dappled or partial sun; Torrey's mountain mint favors open woodland edges and is often stunted by full, unrelieved sun.

directions: Plant in dry to average, well-drained soil at a woodland margin or dappled-sun opening, where this Appalachian mountain mint performs best; plants sited in hot, unbroken full sun are often noticeably stunted compared with those given light shade for part of the day. Small, tightly clustered white flowers open from June into October, drawing an exceptional variety of native bees, wasps, and butterflies over an unusually long season, much like its better-known mountain mint relatives. The aromatic, narrow foliage is deer- and rabbit-resistant, and clumps spread slowly by rhizomes to form modest colonies rather than aggressive patches. Because it is ranked globally imperiled and is state-endangered across much of its range, gardeners should source only nursery-propagated stock and consider it a valuable, conservation-minded addition to pollinator or native woodland-edge plantings.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall, or direct sow seed in fall for cold stratification, into average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; whorled mountain mint spreads by rhizomes and appreciates protection from the hottest afternoon sun in warmer parts of its range.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where afternoon shade can moderate the hottest summer days; whorled mountain mint reaches its full three-foot height in average soil and full sun but stays shorter and more compact in drier or shadier spots. Stem tips are topped from July through September by dense whorled clusters of small white flowers speckled with pink and purple, drawing a remarkable diversity of bees, wasps, and butterflies over an extended bloom window. The finely aromatic foliage is deer- and rabbit-resistant, and established clumps spread steadily by rhizomes, so give it room in a meadow planting or be prepared to root-prune it annually in a more formal border. It is a reliable, easy-care choice for rocky slopes, open woodland edges, and pollinator meadows across its native eastern range.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring, or direct sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification, into average, medium to medium-wet soil in full sun to half shade; Appalachian mountain mint spreads moderately into wider clumps over time and adapts to a range of soil types.

directions: Plant in average to medium-wet soil in full sun to half shade; this Southern Appalachian native tolerates a wide range of soil types and forms an upright clump that spreads moderately with age. Early-season foliage is glossy dark green, while the uppermost leaves develop a powdery silver-reddish cast as small white flower clusters open from June or July into August, attracting a broad range of native bees, wasps, and butterflies. The strongly aromatic leaves are ignored by deer and rabbits, and the dried flower heads persist into fall, adding textural interest after bloom. Appalachian mountain mint is well suited to woodland-edge meadows, pollinator borders, and naturalized plantings across its native mountain range from Virginia and West Virginia south to Georgia and Alabama.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Bigelow's sneezeweed is native to seasonally wet meadows and streamsides of California and Oregon and performs best where soil moisture never fully dries out.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, replicating the mountain meadows and streamside seeps of California and southern Oregon where this species grows wild. Bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads with reflexed rays and a prominent dark purple-brown central disk open on tall, sturdy stems from mid to late summer, standing well above a basal rosette of foliage. The blooms draw abundant bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, making this an excellent choice for rain gardens, pond margins, and other reliably damp, sunny sites where many other sneezeweeds struggle. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Sow seed or plant corm divisions into moist to average, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Garber's blazing star grows wild in the pine flatwoods of peninsular Florida and the Bahamas and needs excellent drainage paired with periodic moisture.

directions: Plant into moist to average, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, mimicking the seasonally damp pine flatwoods of peninsular Florida that are this species' native habitat. Growing from a corm, it sends up a comparatively short flower stalk topped with rose-purple blazing-star spikes from late summer into fall, later and often lower-growing than many of its taller inland relatives. The nectar-rich flowers are a valuable late-season resource for bees and migrating butterflies, including monarchs staging through Florida in autumn. It performs best where soil stays lightly moist through the growing season but drains freely, and it combines well with other flatwoods natives such as wiregrass and blazing-star companions in restoration or pollinator plantings.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start divisions in spring, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; larkspur-leaf tickseed is native to open pine woodlands and roadsides of the Southeastern coastal plain and adapts readily to average garden conditions.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where this Southeastern native forms an upright clump with distinctive, deeply divided foliage reminiscent of true larkspur. Bright golden-yellow, red-centered flowers open in loose branching clusters from mid to late summer, well after many earlier-blooming tickseeds have finished, extending nectar availability for bees and small butterflies into the season's second half. It tolerates the lean, dry-to-average soils of open pine woodlands and roadside verges without need for fertilizing, and generally stays upright without staking. Larkspur-leaf tickseed is uncommon in cultivation but well suited to native plant borders, pollinator meadows, and naturalistic plantings across its Southeastern range from Virginia to the Carolinas and Georgia.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile
University of South Florida Plant Atlas
